about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

equation.name: How quickly the air thins with height

H.name: height over which the pressure falls to a third

source.text: Catling, D. C. and Kasting, J. F. 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabited and Lifeless Worlds, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: How quickly the air thins as you climb. Every scale height up, the pressure drops to about a third.
explain.science: Isothermal hydrostatic atmosphere of an ideal gas. Mean molecular weight in atomic mass units (Earth air 28.97).

references: Catling, D. C. and Kasting, J. F. 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabited and Lifeless Worlds, Cambridge University Press, chapters 2 and 4. doi:10.1017/9781139020558

equation.name: Weight of the air pressing on the ground
equation.formula: P = M * g / (4 * pi * R * R)

source.text: Catling, D. C. and Kasting, J. F. 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabited and Lifeless Worlds, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Air pressure is the weight of all the air above you, spread over the ground.
explain.science: Hydrostatic surface pressure of a thin atmosphere (thickness much less than the radius), with gravity taken as constant with height.

references: Catling, D. C. and Kasting, J. F. 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabited and Lifeless Worlds, Cambridge University Press, chapters 2 and 4. doi:10.1017/9781139020558
Chamberlain, J. W. and Hunten, D. M. 1987, Theory of Planetary Atmospheres, 2nd edn, Academic Press
atoms.shown: λ = G M m / (k T r)

equation.name: How tightly a world holds its gas
equation.formula: lambda = G * M * (mp * m_u) / (k * T * r)

r.name: distance from the centre to the top of the air

T.name: temperature at the top of the air

mp.name: mass of the gas particle (atomic mass units)

lambda.name: how tightly the gas is held

source.text: Chamberlain, J. W. and Hunten, D. M. 1987, Theory of Planetary Atmospheres, 2nd edn, Academic Press

explain.curious: Compares how tightly a world holds a gas molecule with how fast heat makes it move. Below about 1.5 the gas pours away; above about 30 it stays for billions of years.
explain.science: Escape parameter at the exobase: gravitational energy over thermal energy for a particle of the given mass (atomic mass units). The Jeans escape flux is n v₀ (1 + λ) e^(-λ) / (2√π), with v₀ the most probable speed.
